II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00531
The full complexity of this situation is anything but obvious. To see it, one must spend many years not only with books, but also with people.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00532

What is at stake is nothing less than our understanding of Islam, together with an entire view of human destiny. It is striking that the very features that seem essential to Shiite spirituality, and which we have only briefly outlined here, have so far escaped the notice of Western readers and most Sunni Muslims alike.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00533

In the coming chapters, then, we shall ask Haydar Amoli how he understands the Shiite texts that use Adam's story to express the human condition. Seen in this light, certain conversations between the First Imam, Ali ibn Abi Talib, and his chosen disciple Kumayl ibn Ziyad take on a new meaning. They seem already to foreshadow the entire destiny of Shiism. They also stand in sharp contrast to the “impossible syntheses” we heard described earlier, in the painful admissions of a Sunni Arab figure from Jordan.
II. Understanding the Shiism of the Twelve Imams
passage-en-00534

In short, Haydar Amoli, Mulla Sadra Shirazi, and later the teachers of the Shaykhi school help us understand both the positions at issue and what is still at stake in what we have called the spiritual struggle of Shiism.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00535
Chapter III The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
en-book-1-ch-3-s1
1. The Position of Shiite Spiritual Thinkers
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00536

Twelver Shiism has often seemed to stand in opposition to the world around it. It has faced fierce hostility that has rarely let up. This hostility was directed against the First Imam himself, and it marked the tragic lives of his eleven descendants.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00537

Yet the Imams warned their followers from the beginning that their cause would be difficult. To remain faithful to it, they would need “hearts tested by faith.” As a distinguished shaykh once told me, “Never forget that only a handful of people remained faithful to our Imams. It will be like that until the end of this age.” In Shiite understanding, the tradition bears witness to the full spiritual meaning of Islam's prophetic message. For that reason, it could not make peace with the world's ambitions and designs.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00538

Our purpose here is not to write a political history. We only need to understand why so many traces of Shiite life disappear from the historical record. This was especially true after the Seljuk Turks entered Baghdad in 1055, ending the influence of the Persian Shiite Buyid dynasty. For centuries, Shiites lived discreetly, observing strict rules about keeping their beliefs and teachings hidden. Even today, we may have difficulty deciding whether a particular writer was Shiite.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00539
We can sense an admission between the lines, but it was something the author could not safely say openly.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00540
An anonymous Persian treatise from the seventh Islamic century (the thirteenth century CE) expresses this frustration with remarkable force. Its author writes:
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00541

Suppose someone asks why the teachings of the Sunni legal scholars, the fuqaha, have spread so widely, while the teachings of the holy Imams—the Ahl al-Bayt, the members of the Prophet's household—have not. Here is the answer. When Muawiya, the first Umayyad ruler, seized power over the Muslim community, he gave free rein to his hatred of the Commander of the Faithful, the First Imam, Ali ibn Abi Talib. He wrote to his governors, ordering them to put to death anyone who followed Ali's religion. ... People even cursed Ali from the pulpits of the mosques. ... The same hatred pursued the Imam's descendants, making it difficult for them to teach or gather students.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00542
We are told that when Sufyan al-Thawri visited the Sixth Imam, Jafar al-Sadiq, the Imam said to him: “Sufyan, the Abbasid police are looking for you, and the ruler has his eye on you. Leave quickly!
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00543

“But understand that we are not sending you away.” And when Abu Hanifa, the founder of the Hanafi school of Sunni law, had to refer to the Commander of the Faithful in his lessons, he would say only, “The shaykh said this ...”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00544

Things did not improve when Umayyad rule ended and the Abbasids came to power in 132 AH (750 CE). The Imams had to remain inside their homes and practise taqiyya: discretion, or the careful concealment of teachings that could put them in danger. No one could freely come to help them or receive a riwaya, a transmitted teaching, from them. ... Meanwhile, every opportunity was given to the legal scholars who opposed the Imams. Their hatred and ignorance brought them honours.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00545

Each was given a province (wilayat) in which he could spread his teaching as he pleased. All this is well known. Let anyone with wisdom reflect on it. If something of the Imams' teaching is still found everywhere today, despite all these obstacles, surely that proves that God protects the religion of His Messenger, the community of our Imams, and their knowledge.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00546

This bleak picture gives us some sense of what Shiites endured at the hands of the religious establishment backed by political power. The Tenth and Eleventh Imams lived virtually as prisoners in the military camp at Samarra, about a hundred kilometres north of Baghdad. Both died while still young.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00547
Yet they too had fearless students, to whom they passed on their teaching, as the great encyclopedia of Majlisi, mentioned earlier, shows.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00548

The anonymous thirteenth-century writer ends on a note that captures something essential in the Shiite outlook: what we might call desperatio fiducialis, a despair that still trusts. He lived during the upheaval of the Mongol invasions, in the age of the Shiite philosopher and theologian Nasir al-Din Tusi and the Shiite Sufi master Sad al-Din Hamuyah.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00549

In the following century came the writings of Haydar Amoli and Rajab Borsi. Later still, in the century before the rise of the Safavids, came the work of Ibn Abi Jumhur, whom we have already met. If further proof were needed, this history would offer another example of the saying that “the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the faithful.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00550

But when we speak of the spiritual struggle of Shiism, we are not thinking primarily of this open conflict, in which everyone can easily identify who belongs to which side. We mean something subtler: a struggle against a danger arising from within. This danger is harder to recognise because, as we have just seen in the preceding pages, it takes shape at the very moment when everything outwardly seems to be going well.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00551

From the outside, one might hardly expect danger to grow out of a success as striking as the rise of the Safavids in Iran. It did not, at least, begin with Shah Ismail himself. He was a Sufi, surrounded by Sufi companions. At fifteen, after entering Tabriz in triumph, he boldly had the prayer recited in the great mosque in the name of the holy Imams, despite the hostility of the city's Sunni population. At that time, the Safavid family had many ties with the Nimatullahi family, descended from Shah Nimatullah Wali of Kerman, one of the great masters of Shiite Sufism (died 834 AH/1431 CE).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00552

But the situation changed profoundly under Shah Abbas the Great (1587–1628). We are not concerned here with the history of his reign. What matters is what happened to people devoted to the spiritual life. Mulla Sadra Shirazi's personal remarks in his books—and the reasons he wrote several of those books—tell us enough about that. We shall return to him in Book V.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00553

The Safavid revival brought an extraordinary flowering of thought, unlike anything else then found in the Islamic world. Several schools arose whose influence can still be felt today. Their leading figures included Mir Damad, Sadra Shirazi, Mohsen Fayz, Rajab Ali Tabrizi, and many others, followed in turn by generations of students.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00554

But this does not mean their lives were easy. Mulla Sadra tells us why he spent about ten years in seclusion in a small village hidden high in a valley near Qom: the hostility of the fuqaha, the legal scholars, and their refusal to engage with hikmat (philosophical and spiritual wisdom) or irfan (inner spiritual knowledge).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00555
We now encounter the paradox we began to describe a few pages ago. Shiite spiritual knowledge had survived centuries of persecution and concealment.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00556

Yet with Shiism's worldly success, it faced a new kind of trial. Human affairs took their familiar course. Alongside the exceptional achievements of the great sages, the hukama, there grew an increasingly powerful religious establishment centred on law. It became more and more concerned with the practical details of religious rules, legal judgments, and individual cases, and increasingly suspicious of philosophy, divine wisdom, and mystical experience. Strictly speaking, it is difficult to talk about a clergy where there is no Church.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00557
Yet the fuqaha and the akhunds—the religious scholars and teachers—have sometimes filled that role so thoroughly that the consequences are still felt today.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00558

Mulla Sadra is not our only witness. The lack of understanding later shown towards the Shaykhi school offers another example; we shall discuss it in Book VI. I can say that even today, in Iran, the dominance of fiqh (Islamic religious law) and the fuqaha is a frequent subject of quiet conversation among the hukama (sages) and the urafa (those devoted to inner spiritual knowledge). How did things reach this point? How did the study of religious law come to occupy so much ground?
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00559

Of course, the study of law forms part of every philosopher-theologian's education. The problem arises with legal scholars who claim that all theological knowledge can be reduced to fiqh. In doing so, they cut away part of the Imams' own teaching and prevent Shiism from making its spiritual message known.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00560

But keeping that message alive and passing it on has nothing to do with whether a particular Muslim society decides to introduce a civil legal code in order to “adapt to the modern world.” When the whole of Islamic learning is narrowed to the study of religious law, the result is a dead end.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00561

This is no doubt a familiar pattern in the social history of religion, and not only in Islam. The rejection of spiritual insight, or gnosis, grows out of a rigid reliance on reason that often conceals an unwillingness—or an inability—to recognise what lies beyond it. The result is the situation we described earlier: Shiism is almost forced to hide from itself. Its own tradition of inner spiritual knowledge must retreat from official Shiism in order to survive intact.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00562

Yet from the beginning, Shiism understood itself as the inner meaning of the prophetic message (batin al-nubuwwa). In the moving words of Imam Jafar, it was the religion of the strangers, the ghuraba, within Muhammad's community. That worldly triumph should have produced an official Shiism that in turn makes strangers of the Imam's own strangers—this is what gives the “spiritual struggle of Shiism” its meaning.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00563

It is for Shiism itself to carry that struggle through and overcome the predicament described by the Jordanian public figure in the interview we discussed earlier (pp. 32 onward). The age of outward triumph has already passed. Only those who understand the Imam's call will be able to meet the immense questions raised within Shiite Islam, as elsewhere, by the influence of the West. And this is not simply a problem facing traditional Islam in what is called the modern world. It faces everyone, wherever they live, who still senses that human beings have a spiritual destiny beyond this earthly life.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00564

Iranian Islam has never lacked people willing to take up this struggle, generation after generation, right down to our own time. Earlier, we said that Shiite spiritual thinkers had to fight on two fronts. Haydar Amoli's writings show that one of these fronts was itself divided in two, because Sufism could be understood in two very different ways. It could be seen as a witness to Shiism within the Sunni world, or as a movement that had broken away and forgotten its beginnings.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00565

To understand this, we must return to a particular kind of Shiite spiritual thinker. Such people use much the same specialised language as the Sufis, and their teaching about divine wisdom is familiar enough that many non-Shiite Sufis can readily find their way through it. They too have dreams and visionary experiences. Yet they do not belong to Sufism as an organised movement.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00566

This was precisely the situation that led Mulla Sadra, on one side, to confront legal scholars who dismissed spiritual wisdom and, on the other, to write a treatise against certain Sufis of his day. These Sufis professed a kind of pious refusal to seek knowledge. They scorned books and rejected philosophical reflection as a spiritual practice. In the end, this attitude could become a kind of spiritual licence: the opposite error to that of the legal scholars. Instead of giving all importance to the outward form of religion, they readily claimed to possess its inner meaning (batin) without needing its outward form (zahir).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00567

The mystical philosophers of the Shaykhi school also criticised Sufism. One of their objections concerned the way some Sufis understood wahdat al-wujud, the idea that “being” has one meaning wherever we encounter it.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00568

But their criticism was directed above all at Sufi orders (tariqat), their collective practices, and the authority given to the Sufi shaykh or master. For these Shiite thinkers, Shiism itself, understood in its fullness, is already the spiritual path in the highest sense. A separate Sufi master therefore seems to take the place of the one spiritual guide a Shiite should acknowledge and follow: the Hidden Imam, who cannot be seen by the senses but is present to the heart. We might compare the role of a Sufi shaykh here with that of a guru in India.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00569
These thinkers shared the view Haydar Amoli had expressed much earlier: that Sufism first arose within Islam through Shiism, but lost its true nature when it broke away from the Shiite Imams.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00570

Indeed, it is as though Sunni Sufism transferred the teaching about the Imams onto the person of the Prophet alone, leaving out whatever did not fit Sunni belief. Take the Sufi idea of the mystical Pole, the Qutb: it is essentially the idea of the Imam. In Shiite Sufism, the Imam remains the Pole of poles, because he is the Seal of walayat, the highest spiritual guidance and closeness to God. In Sunni Sufism, the Qutb takes the place occupied by the Imam in Shiite thought.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00571

We can already see signs of this relationship during the third and fourth Islamic centuries (the ninth and tenth centuries CE), when the great works of Ismaili spiritual philosophy began to appear. The question becomes even more pointed when Sunni Sufis present themselves as bearers of a message from the Hidden Imam.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00572
Consider al-Hallaj. He cannot simply be separated from the people whose technical language he adopted: no one borrows a set of words without taking something of its meaning.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00573

Yet it seems that people tried to distance him from them in order to discredit those very people. The more sharply he is separated from them, however, the more this seems to support the Shiite judgment of his case.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00574

We should also remember Jabir ibn Hayyan, the famous alchemist. According to a long-established tradition that has never been decisively disproved, he was a disciple of Imam Jafar al-Sadiq. From early on he was known as the Sufi. Jabir's alchemy cannot be separated from his Shiite ideas: the Imam plays the same role in the spiritual world that the Stone or the Elixir plays in the world of Nature. One of Jabir's most difficult works may even contain the earliest developed expression of a genuinely spiritual theme: the Stranger, the one who comes from elsewhere, the spiritual exile (gharib) who has travelled from distant shores.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00575

In Shiite spiritual thought, the model for this Stranger is Salman the Persian (Salman Parsi), also called Salman the Pure (Salman Pak). He was a pilgrim searching for the true Prophet. Born into the chivalric tradition of the Zoroastrian religion, he passed through Christianity before finding what he understood as pure, spiritual Islam. Alone and without family, he became the adopted son of the Imam.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00576

Salman's story is also the story of everyone addressed by Imam Jafar's celebrated saying. We must quote it again, because it serves almost as a guiding motto: “Islam began as a stranger, and it will become a stranger again, just as it was at the beginning. Blessed are those within Muhammad's community who become strangers—the ghuraba.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00577

As we already know, these words rule out any simple equation between religion and society. The Imam is not calling people to a merely social religion. By blessing the spiritual exile, he calls that person to refuse compromises with the accepted values and structures of this world. Instead, the world itself becomes the setting for a quest for another world. It becomes the place of a journey towards what is already invisibly present within it: the world of rebirth and Resurrection, which the Imam announces.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00578

If we want to use today's fashionable language, we might say that this is the only true way for the spiritual pilgrim, as a witness to what is absolute, to be “present in the world” or “committed” to it. This is the spiritual Islam whose existence went unnoticed not only by the Jordanian figure whose moving testimony we discussed earlier, but also by the many people whose thinking that testimony sadly represents today.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00579

Imam Jafar's saying, by contrast, describes a person's encounter with the last things—death, resurrection, and the life beyond—as something that can be lived now, in the present. Choosing spiritual exile in order to follow the Imam is a decisive break. It ends a kind of captivity: the safety offered by the walls society builds around individuals to protect them from a direct religious experience. Once those walls are broken, a person suddenly becomes conscious of ghurbat, of being in exile. Suhrawardi will give this discovery unforgettable form in a story we shall examine in Book II.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00580

The Imam's words call his follower into walayat: a devoted love for the pure figures through whom God makes Himself known. Their light draws the person out of the loneliness of exile. It also exposes all the falsehoods that have disguised the reality of that exile and encouraged a comfortable compromise with this world. This is why Haydar Amoli still speaks directly to Shiite spiritual life today. His work awakens readers to a threefold spiritual struggle, a struggle on three fronts, which they must face if they are to answer the Imam's call and remain faithful to Shiism in its fullness.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00581

We already know two of these three fronts. The first is the struggle with Sunnism insofar as it is treated as a religion concerned only with sharia, the outward religious law. In this form, its legal authorities refuse to let the law come alive through its inner spiritual truth. The disagreement is clear enough. It becomes clearer still when “modernising the sharia” turns religious law into a merely social religion.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00582

The second struggle is more painful, because it takes place within Shiism itself. Here the urafa and hukama—spiritual seekers and sages who remain faithful to the whole teaching of the holy Imams—find themselves opposed by legal scholars who profess Shiism outwardly but have forgotten its calling. They have forgotten the Imams' teaching about the inner meaning of revelation, through which the prophetic message is deepened and transformed.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00583

Finally, there is an even subtler struggle with a certain kind of Sufism that has forgotten its own roots. By turning away from Shiism, forgetting where walayat begins, and losing sight of who is its Seal, it mistakes the source of spiritual authority. And by giving too much attention to particular techniques at the expense of irfan, genuine spiritual understanding, it risks sinking into a pious darkness that can no longer answer people's questions or meet their deepest hopes.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00584

As we shall see in Book IV, Haydar Amoli's great work has precisely this aim: to persuade the legal scholars that mystical knowledge (irfan) is necessary, and to bring back those Sufis who have become, in a sense, lost witnesses to Shiism within Sunni Islam. Only then can the original relationship between Sufism and Shiism be restored.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00585

For Haydar Amoli, the very survival of spiritual Islam depends on this. Writing in the fourteenth century, he had already seen with extraordinary clarity the problems that would become increasingly urgent as Shiism developed in Iran. And the way he stated those problems still matters to anyone who understands what is at stake in this threefold struggle: the divine trust placed in human hands.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
en-book-1-ch-3-s2
2. The Divine Trust Given to Humanity
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00586

At heart, the question is this: if we remove the batin—the hidden, inner, spiritual meaning—from Islamic teaching, do we remove something without which the whole teaching loses its meaning? And is the teaching of the Shiite Imams precisely this inner dimension of Islam, an essential part of what it means for a religion to have a revealed holy book?
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00587

For the Imams themselves are understood to embody the inner reality of the Muhammadan Word, the eternal prophetic Reality (Haqiqat Muhammadiya). From the beginning, then, the full reality of a revealed Book requires both zahir and batin: its outward meaning and its inner meaning.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00588

This explains why Haydar Amoli takes the same position as Shiite sages and spiritual seekers everywhere. He challenges two groups at once. On one side are Shiites who reject the spiritual knowledge found in Sufism because they have forgotten its Shiite origins. On the other are Sufis who attack Shiism because they have forgotten those same origins.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00589

Both groups act as though they do not know that the teachings of the holy Imams contain the secrets of the highest forms of knowledge. Both have set this side of the teaching aside, insisting that the Imams were concerned only with outward religious matters: the observance of the law, religious rites, and legal judgments.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00590

Some have even suggested that, if the Imams possessed a secret teaching, they never passed it on to anyone. Certain Shiite legal scholars have argued this way in order to deny that any inner teaching exists. Certain Sufis have done so in order to disown their own beginnings, forgetting that without Shiism and the Imams, their philosophy of divine wisdom would not exist. We shall examine the relevant texts in Book IV, section 1.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00591

The Imams were not merely interpreters of the sharia. Or rather, it was through the way they interpreted it that they became guides along the spiritual path (tariqat) and teachers of its deepest truth (haqiqat). Shaykh Ahmad Ahsai and the Shaykhi school, from the eighteenth century to the present, have argued for nothing different. Their spiritual struggle follows the same direction as Haydar Amoli's.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00592

The Twelve Imams are understood as primordial manifestations of God. Before appearing on earth, they exist as spiritual beings who take part in the very coming-into-being of the worlds (as we saw in Chapter II). These are not merely speculative ideas invented by later thinkers. They are stated in the earliest transmitted teachings, the hadith, including those collected in Kulayni's Kitab al-Hujja.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00593

Just as Christian interpretations of the Bible cannot ignore the place of Christ, Shiite interpretations of the Qur'an necessarily centre on the Imam. The teaching about the Imams contains the secret of both God and humanity—that is, the secret of the relationship between them. According to this vision, the relationship could only be established through “people of light,” the figures designated as prophets.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00594

The manifestation of the Twelve Imams—or, more exactly, of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones—takes place as a descent through successive worlds. Each stage is like a new form in which the divine Word appears, much as in the Acts of John, where the Word appears in different forms. A complete interpretation of the revealed Book must therefore take account of all these levels of existence, from the highest down to the world of earthly human life. We shall return to them in Chapter V.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00595

Many sayings traditionally attributed to the Prophet and the Imams make the same point. They explain hints found in Qur'anic verses and show, in this understanding, that Islam and the Qur'anic revelation require an inner teaching: a higher truth that remains hidden. We could also examine the many sermons (khutbas) attributed to individual Imams. In these sermons, however, it is really the eternal Imam who speaks, and each of the Twelve Imams is an earthly expression of that one reality, for they all share a single essence.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00596

One of the most striking examples is the famous Sermon of the Declaration (Khutbat al-Bayan). Here the Imam identifies himself with the Perfect Human Being (Anthropos teleios). In doing so, Shiite teaching about the Imams connects with the ancient spiritual image of the Heavenly Human, found in earlier traditions of inner knowledge. The sermon contains seventy statements. Repeated one after another with growing force, they are said to have carried the audience into a trance when the First Imam delivered them at Kufa. Here are just a few:
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00597

I am the Sign of the Almighty. I am the First and the Last. I am the One Who Is Revealed and the One Who Is Hidden. I am the Face of God. I am the Hand of God. I am the Side of God. I am the one called Elijah in the Gospel. I am the one who holds the secret of God's Messenger. ...
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00598

This vision of the Imam as a manifestation of God leads Shiite writers such as Haydar Amoli to find in the Qur'an itself a command to exercise discretion: taqiyya, or kitman, the duty to keep certain truths concealed.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00599

We must be clear about what this means. It is not simply the practice of saying something while silently meaning the opposite. It certainly offers a means of protection, and the reasons Shiites needed that protection are easy to understand. But above all, it follows a demanding principle of spiritual honesty.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00600

If the Qur'an teaches this honesty, that is because there is both an outer and an inner meaning to religious truth. It is fitting that the instruction itself should be expressed in a veiled form. This is the inner sense of verses that speak of a trust which must be returned only to someone entitled to receive it.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00601

One verse in particular says: “God commands you to restore the trusts placed in your hands to those to whom they belong” (4:61). Haydar Amoli explains that all God's secrets (asrar Allah), all the hidden truths of divine wisdom, are trusts placed in the hearts of God's friends (awliya). To disclose them to someone unprepared to receive them is to break both the religious law and God's command. This is why the Imams themselves told their followers to observe taqiyya.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00602

The idea of an entrusted secret also brings us to the story of Adam, the earthly human being, and to the drama that begins with him. The very possibility of revealing a secret to the wrong person—and of disobeying the instruction to pass it on only to its rightful heir—takes us to the heart of the holy Book and of spiritual wisdom. One Qur'anic verse is so important that the whole reason for an inner religious teaching can be said to depend on it. For the verse joins the mystery of God to the mystery of humanity, as though they were one and the same mystery. God declares:
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00603

We offered the trust of Our secrets to the heavens, the earth, and the mountains. They all refused to carry it; they all trembled at receiving it. But the human being accepted the burden, for he is violent and ignorant. (Qur'an 33:72)
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00604
To understand this verse, we must answer two questions.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00605

First, what is the trust? What secrets does it contain? Second, what do the human being's violence and ignorance—or lack of awareness—mean here? The questions cannot be separated. What sort of secrets could a person have accepted only by being violent and ignorant? And how could those very qualities lead that person to betray the trust? This violence and ignorance have a troubling double meaning. Shiite interpretation finds in them the drama from which the human condition, as we know it now, arose: the secret of humanity's present destiny.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00606

To do this subject justice, we would need to bring together all the Shiite traditions and all the sayings of the Imams that touch, directly or indirectly, on this verse. That would require an entire book.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00607
Let us give only the briefest outline. The Imams repeatedly explain the verse by saying, “That secret was our walayat.”
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00608

But walayat, their spiritual authority and closeness to God, is itself part of a threefold acknowledgment: of the oneness of the one God (tawhid); of the prophets' outward mission (nubuwwat); and of the inner mission of God's friends (walayat). The burden humanity accepted was this threefold testimony (shahadat).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00609

Yet this threefold testimony—especially its second and third parts—assumes the existence of a humanity made entirely of light: a higher, heavenly humanity that existed before Adam and the earthly human race. That is why the full meaning of the Qur'anic verse can be understood only within the whole Shiite vision of how the worlds began and how prophecy came into existence. Within that larger vision, Adam's violence and ignorance have two sides. One brings him praise; the other brings about his downfall. Recognising both sides allows us to see how the different Shiite explanations of the verse fit together.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00610
Let us try to make these closely packed ideas a little clearer.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00611

We must keep in mind two sayings, one attributed to the Prophet and the other to the Imam: “I was already a prophet ...” and “I was already a wali, an Imam, when Adam was still between water and clay.” In other words, they existed before Adam had even been formed.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00612

According to this teaching, before the humanity descended from earthly Adam, there was already another humanity. Its existence reaches unimaginably further back than anything the sciences could call prehistory. This is a humanity of pure light, like the seraphim: beings untouched by any fall, immaculate and free from error, unlike earthly human beings. They form the complete company of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones (Chahardeh Masum).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00613

Our texts, including the commentaries of Qazi Said Qummi, give them revealing names: the supreme humanity, the humanity of the heights (al-bashar al-awali), the archangelic humanity (anas aqliyun), the people of light (bashar nuriyun), and others. In their longing and the rapture of their love (walah wa hayaman), these beings of light surround the sublime Throne: the invisible Temple that serves as the model for every temple in every universe. Many sayings of the Prophet and the Imams refer to this existence before earthly humanity. The idea shapes the whole Shiite account of the origin of the worlds and of human nature.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00614
Among these sayings is an exceptionally long conversation between the Fifth Imam, Muhammad al-Baqir, and his disciple Jabir al-Jufi.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00615

We can give only the main outlines of this magnificent hadith. It begins with the teaching we have already encountered: the Prophet and the Imams were the first beings created. At that time, there was no heaven or earth, no place, no night or day, no sun or moon, no Adam and no earthly humanity.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00616

The Fourteen Immaculate Ones came forth as Fourteen Lights—fourteen beings of light, or aeons. Their relationship to their Lord's light is like the relationship between the sun's rays and the sun itself. The picture even recalls the emerald vision in the Book of Revelation. The Fourteen Lights surround the Presence that words cannot describe, like fourteen green canopies: “Around the throne was a rainbow that looked like an emerald” (Revelation 4:3).
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00617

From this complete company of Fourteen Lights, the worlds come into existence in the following order: first the Place of places, then the cosmic Throne, then the heavens and the angels, then the air and the spirits or jinn, and finally Adam, the earthly human being. At every stage in the creation of the worlds, the threefold testimony (shahadat) appears again, in one mysterious form or another. It affirms God's absolute oneness (tawhid), the prophets' mission (nubuwwat), and the Imams' role in guiding people towards the inner truth (walayat). This is because every stage of creation has its own manifestation of the Fourteen Lights.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00618
The creation of the worlds and of humanity ends with a solemn enthronement of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. God addresses them:
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00619

It was for your sake that I created what I have created. You are the chosen ones whom I have placed between Myself and My creation. Through you I have hidden Myself from all My creatures other than you. I have made you the means by which they come into My presence, and through you every request is addressed to Me. For everything is destined to perish except My Face (see Qur'an 55:26–27), and you are My Face. You do not perish, and neither will those who choose you as their friends.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00620

This solemn passage is a good example of what is called a hadith qudsi: a sacred saying in which God speaks in the first person, as He does in the Qur'an. Its form becomes understandable within the wider Shiite teaching about how prophetic knowledge is received, which we shall examine in Chapter VI.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00621

What the saying tells us is that the Fourteen beings of light are the original figures through whom God is made known. They make divine manifestation itself possible. For the God who is beyond all reach, “creating the world” means becoming known. And He can be known only through these figures, because whichever way we turn, they are the divine Face we encounter.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00622

Human beings can know God only through His Names and Attributes; the Fourteen provide the forms in which those Names and Attributes can be recognised. This is why they are called Hujjat—the surety, the proof, the ones who stand as witnesses. The Fourteen Immaculate Ones stand for the God whom nobody can see or reach. That is why they are His imperishable Face. Later, in Chapter VII, we shall see that this is the very secret of why the Imam stands at the centre of Shiite spiritual life.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00623

Many other traditions confirm this account. Some were collected by Shaykh Saduq Ibn Babuyeh. They describe the Prophet and the Imam as two primordial Spirits who form a single Light: a unity with two sides, expressing the two dimensions of the Haqiqat Muhammadiya, the eternal Muhammadan Reality.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00624

The implication is that the higher humanity belonging to the Muhammadan Word, or Muhammadan Light (Nur Muhammadi), existed before Adam and the human race descended from him. The meaning of this higher humanity becomes clearer when God decides to create earthly Adam. The Creator takes a portion of this Light and kneads it together with a portion of the “clay” of Illiyyun, the highest level of paradise. This substance of light is then placed within Adam.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00625

It becomes the divine side (jihat haqiqiya, the lahut) of the prophets' being, alongside their human, created side (jihat khalqiya, the nasut). Through the first, the prophets receive from God. Through the second, they communicate with human beings. The light placed in Adam passes from prophet to prophet until the last stage in the cycle of prophecy. With Abd al-Muttalib, the common grandfather of the Prophet Muhammad and Imam Ali, this one light divides into two halves. One appears in Muhammad as the Seal of Prophecy. The other appears in Ali as the Seal of walayat, the completion of the Imams' spiritual authority and guidance.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00626
Of course, this light is not passed on through any process taking place in the physical body.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00627

We must understand its transmission in terms of the “subtle body,” the spiritual form of a person rather than the body of flesh. It points towards the only sense in which Islamic teachings about the prophets could accept the idea of “incarnation.” It also recalls a very specific idea from early Christianity, particularly Jewish Christianity and the Ebionites: the “True Prophet,” who moves swiftly from one prophet to the next until reaching his final resting place. For Christians, that resting place is Jesus; in Islam, it is Muhammad.
III. The Spiritual Struggle of Shiism
passage-en-00628

With these ideas in mind, we can begin to see what secret was entrusted to Adam, the human being, and how the very lack of awareness that allowed him to accept such a responsibility also led him to betray it.
